newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin gets tough with Russia's tax dodgers.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin gets tough with Russia's tax dodgers.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin told Russians on Friday they must pay their taxes to end the suffering of millions of unpaid public sector workers as the government's budget plans were roundly rejected by parliament.

"Payment of salaries and pensions is not only a question of politics and economy. It is also a question of conscience," the 65-year-old president said in a seven-minute radio address from the sanatorium where he is preparing for heart bypass surgery.

The businesslike performance, eight days after Yeltsin told people in a first radio broadcast not to write him off, preempted an attack from his former bodyguard and friend, Alexander Korzhakov, who accused the new Kremlin team of deliberately running the president into the ground.
Korzhakov's statement was the latest bout of mudslinging as senior figures jockey for position in Yeltsin's absence.

Speaking clearly and coherently, Yeltsin announced the creation of a special tax-collection commission and appointed Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to head it, with Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais as his deputy.
"I may assure pensioners and the workers of budget sphere, policemen and servicemen. Pensions and salaries will be paid. I, as president, am confident of it," he said.

The new commission could meet as early as Monday and will group representatives of the federal security and intelligence services and state prosecutors as well as the financial authorities, Chubais told Interfax news agency.
"We can no longer endure a situation where the poor grow poorer and the rich get richer by breaking Russian laws...The state will use all its power to put a stop to this," he said.
The government, which has said tax collection is well short of target this year, was unable to persuade parliament, which is dominated by communists, that its plans for 1997 made sense.
The State Duma lower house, sceptical of government revenue forecasts, rejected its draft 1997 budget in a first reading by 280 votes to 33.

Deputies went on to debate whether to order the government to present a new draft within 20 days or to set up a conciliation commission with representatives from both houses of parliament and the government to thrash out the differences.
Yeltsin dramatised his radio plea by drawing attention to Moscow scientist Vladimir Strakhov, who has started a hunger strike to demand funds for his physics institute.

"I am appealing to those of you who do not pay taxes. The fate of this 64-year-old academic is on your conscience. The fate of more than 100 million of our countrymen depends on how taxes are collected," Yeltsin said.

Dismal tax collection has curbed the government's ability to fulfil its spending plans, prompting protests by groups ranging from power workers to actors and fuelling suggestions that the disgruntled, cash-strapped armed forces could mutiny.
Millions of Russians have not been paid for months, despite Yeltsin's promises in his successful campaign for re-election to settle all wage debts.

Yeltsin has been out of the Kremlin for most of the time since he was reelected on July 3, prompting talk of a power struggle. The opposition says the country is rudderless and in chaos, but the bitterest political battle at present appears to involve groups in or close to the Kremlin.
Korzhakov, a 46-year-old general, was once Yeltsin's sports and -- some say -- drinking partner. He was sacked in June along with a number of other hawkish advisers.
Giving his first news conference, which turned into a media scrum, Korzhakov denied accusations of corruption and hit out at Yeltsin's new entourage especially, by inference, Chubais.

Analysts say allegations of multi-million-dollar extortion levelled at Korzhakov this week by a former Kremlin financier may have been launched to sink a budding alliance between him and ambitious national security chief, Alexander Lebed.
